title: When Fresh Information Is Not Enough: Age-of-Actuation-Optimal Scheduling forEnergy-Harvesting Actuators

paper.title: When Fresh Information Is Not Enough: Age-of-Actuation-Optimal Scheduling for Energy-Harvesting Actuators
paper.abstract: Abstract We study transmission scheduling in an energy-harvesting actuation system where an actuation requires both a received update and available energy. While age of information (AoI) measures information freshness, age of actuation (AoA) measures the time elapsed since the latest completed actuation. The transmitter observes the receiver’s AoA and battery state and decides whether to transmit a fresh update in each slot. We formulate average-AoA minimization as a Markov decision process and establish an AoA-threshold property for an optimal policy . We also derive the average AoA in closed form under the AoI-optimal policy, which is always-transmit . Numerical results show that AoA-aware scheduling can improve actuation freshness while reducing the number of transmissions, although information freshness may deteriorate. The two policies coincide for some pairs of channel success and energy-arrival probabilities. For a one-unit battery, the transmission rate under the AoA-optimal policy can vary nonmonotonically with the energy-arrival probability.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Timeliness is a key requirement in many communication systems, such as remote monitoring and networked control. The most widely used metric for it is the Age of Information (AoI). It was originally proposed in [ 2 ] and has since been analyzed in numerous communication systems [ 3 , 4 ] . It is defined, at a destination, as the time elapsed since the generation of the freshest data available at that destination [ 4 ] , i.e., I ⁡ ( t ) = t − u ⁡ ( t ) I(t)=t-u(t) , where u ⁡ ( t ) u(t) denotes the timestamp of the freshest received data, at or before time t t . Unlike delay, it captures both how often updates are sent and how long they take to arrive. However, AoI stops at reception. It implicitly assumes that a received update is immediately useful. In many systems, this is not the case. The received data is used to trigger an action at the destination [ 5 ] , and this action needs more than the data itself: a possibility , an enabling condition to put data into use. For example, an actuator powered by harvested energy can act only if its battery holds enough energy. An update that arrives when the battery is empty resets the AoI, yet no action takes place. The destination then holds fresh information, but its latest action is old. Moreover, a policy that minimizes the AoI may spend transmissions on updates that never translate into actions. Therefore, the freshness of the received data alone does not characterize the freshness of the actuations. Extensions of AoI have been proposed to capture semantic attributes and goal-oriented aspects of communication [ 6 , 5 ] , such as nonlinear aging costs [ 7 ] , version changes [ 8 ] , incorrect information [ 9 ] , and request- or query-based relevance [ 10 , 11 ] . The closest to actuation is Age of Loop (AoL), which extends AoI to closed-loop control by measuring the time since the generation of the state or command behind the latest applied action [ 12 ] . However, AoL assumes that actuation occurs periodically, with a fixed cycle. It does not model actuation as a constrained possibility that depends on a random process, such as the availability of energy. To capture this, we proposed Age of Actuation (AoA) [ 13 ] and later Age of Actuated Information (AoAI) [ 14 ] to go one step beyond AoI and analyze the broader case in which data requires a certain possibility (e.g., physical or admission-related) at the destination to be effectively utilized, and to assess the freshness of this final outcome. We refer to this concept as actuation . AoA is defined as the time elapsed since the most recent actuation at the destination ; its formal definition, together with that of the AoI, is given in Section II-B .

sections.heading: I-A Related Work
sections.text: In a partial categorization, the analysis and optimization of AoI and, more generally, timeliness metrics can be divided into two main approaches: randomized (state-independent) policies and dynamic (state-dependent) policies.

sections.heading: I-A 1 Randomized Policies
sections.text: They typically enable tractable analytical characterization, often modeling the system as an uncontrolled Markov chain, and can be interpreted as open-loop control. The decision policy is modeled as one or more random variables (RVs), usually Bernoulli RVs. After characterizing the system dynamics, one typically derives a closed-form expression for the timeliness metric (e.g., average AoI) as a function of the corresponding probability parameters of these RVs. In this approach, the policy does not depend on the system state; instead, at each time slot, decisions are made by sampling the RVs independently of the current system conditions [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . In our previous works, we utilized this approach [ 13 , 14 ] .

sections.heading: I-A 2 Dynamic Policies
sections.text: They incorporate feedback from the system state, with decisions made at each time slot based on the current state of the system, such as age, channel conditions, and resource availability, thereby corresponding to closed-loop control. After decisions are made, the system transitions probabilistically to a new state according to its underlying dynamics. This sequential decision-making and the stochastic nature of the system lead to the formulation of the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), which provides a principled framework through the definition of states, actions, transition probabilities, and instant costs, typically correlating the cost with the age and minimizing the long-term cost which corresponds to the average AoI or related timeliness metrics. When the transition probabilities and instant costs are known, optimal policies can be computed using techniques such as value iteration, relative value iteration, or policy iteration, which rely on recursively solving the Bellman optimality equations. This approach has been applied to AoI minimization in energy harvesting systems with multiple sources [ 18 ] , wireless powered systems with joint sampling and updating [ 19 ] , and wireless broadcast networks [ 20 ] , and to version AoI in energy harvesting and caching systems [ 21 , 22 ] . AoI with an energy harvesting source has also been widely studied [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . Transmitting as soon as possible is not always age-optimal [ 28 ] , and this also holds under energy harvesting [ 23 ] . The optimal policy has a threshold structure in the age, shown in discrete time [ 24 ] , for a unit battery [ 25 ] , and for a finite battery with thresholds that decrease with the stored energy [ 26 ] . The average AoI of the greedy policy has also been derived in closed form [ 27 ] . In all these works, the optimized metric measures the freshness of the received data, not of its use. Moreover, in [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] , energy is consumed by the transmission itself. In our model, energy is instead needed at the destination for actuation. As a result, the AoI-optimal policy is to always transmit, and the threshold structure appears in the AoA-optimal policy instead. State-dependent policies have been used to optimize the freshness of received data, but not the freshness of actuation. On the other hand, the AoA has so far been studied only under state-independent randomized policies [ 13 , 14 ] . Thus, it is not known what an AoA-optimal state-dependent policy looks like, and whether and when it differs from the AoI-optimal policy. This paper addresses this gap.

sections.heading: I-B Contribution
sections.text: In this work, we consider a system model that involves state-dependent decision-making to transmit data. We analyze the average AoA and the average AoI under both AoA-Optimal (AoA-Opt.) policy and AoI-Optimal (AoI-Opt.) policy. We thoroughly compare the outcomes and illustrate the trade-offs in timeliness and cost from the perspective of greedy and non-greedy regions, and show how the AoA captures the freshness of completed actuations and can therefore lead to a different optimal transmission policy from the AoI. The main contributions of the paper are as follows: • We characterize the AoA as an average-cost-per-stage problem and derive the optimal average AoA and the corresponding optimal policies using Relative Value Iteration (RVI). • We investigate structural properties of the MDP and prove an AoA-threshold structure for the AoA-Opt. policy , while such a structure for the battery state is observed only numerically. • We characterize the AoA for the AoI-Opt. (always-transmit) policy using a Markov chain formulation, derive its steady-state behavior, and obtain a closed-form expression for the average AoA under this policy. We also establish the ordering among the four values of the average AoA and the average AoI under the two policies. • We present and analyze two sets of operating regions, obtained by comparing the AoA-optimal and AoI-optimal policies, along with the resulting optimal and suboptimal values of the average AoA and the average AoI. • We present counterintuitive system behaviors that emerge at very low battery capacity, namely a battery capacity of one , such as a transmission rate that varies nonmonotonically with the energy-arrival probability. sections.heading: II System Model
sections.text: In this section, we first describe the system dynamics, i.e., the interaction of data transmission, channel success, energy arrivals, the battery, and the actuator over time, and then define the considered timeliness metrics, the AoI and the AoA.

At the transmitter side, there is a time-varying information source containing the data required for actuation. At the beginning of each time slot, the transmitter decides whether or not to transmit the data. This decision is based on the state of the system at the end of the previous time slot. The transmission of data entails sampling the source, generating a packet of information, and transmitting it. This can also be regarded as issuing a command to actuate. sections.heading: V-B Analysis of the Results
sections.text: In this section, we analyze and interpret the results in terms of timeliness and cost. Timeliness is measured by the average AoA and average AoI, while cost refers to the transmission rate required for sensing and transmission. This cost is not explicitly modeled in the problem, as it can be assumed to be negligible compared to the energy consumption associated with actuation and/or of a fundamentally different nature, and is therefore not directly comparable to the actuation energy cost. Figs. 2 , 3 , and 4 show that the average AoA under the AoA-Opt. policy is lower than or equal to that under the AoI-Opt. policy, and conversely, the average AoI under the AoI-Opt. policy is lower than or equal to that under the AoA-Opt. policy. Also, the relation among the four corresponding curves in the plots of Fig. 3 is consistent with ( 33 ). Greedy and Non-Greedy Regions are where the AoA-Opt. policy tends to the AoI-Opt. policy and where it does not, respectively. Notably, this generally occurs for relatively higher values of λ \lambda compared to μ \mu , as can be seen in Figs. 5 and 6 . However, for B m = 1 B_{m}=1 , there is an interesting symmetry around the point μ = λ = 0.5 \mu=\lambda=0.5 , as seen in Fig. 6 . Energy-unlimited and Energy-Limited Regions are where the values of AoA and AoI themselves coincide and where they do not, respectively. sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: We studied transmission scheduling for an energy-harvesting receiver whose actuations require both data and energy. We formulated average-AoA minimization as a Markov decision process and characterized an AoA-threshold optimal policy. We also derived the average AoA in closed form under the AoI-optimal policy, which is always-transmit. Comparing these policies shows that optimizing information freshness alone need not optimize actuation freshness, and that the two policies coincide only for some pairs of channel success and energy-arrival probabilities. State-dependent scheduling can improve average AoA and reduce transmission attempts, although it may increase the average AoI. The numerical results also reveal non-monotonic transmission rates under the AoA-optimal policy for a one-unit battery, illustrating that improved actuation freshness does not require a monotonically increasing transmission rate. An analytical characterization of the observed battery-threshold structure remains an open question.

Abstract We study transmission scheduling in an energy-harvesting actuation system where an actuation requires both a received update and available energy. While age of information (AoI) measures information freshness, age of actuation (AoA) measures the time elapsed since the latest completed actuation. The transmitter observes the receiver’s AoA and battery state and decides whether to transmit a fresh update in each slot. We formulate average-AoA minimization as a Markov decision process and establish an AoA-threshold property for an optimal policy . We also derive the average AoA in closed form under the AoI-optimal policy, which is always-transmit . Numerical results show that AoA-aware scheduling can improve actuation freshness while reducing the number of transmissions, although information freshness may deteriorate. The two policies coincide for some pairs of channel success and energy-arrival probabilities. For a one-unit battery, the transmission rate under the AoA-optimal policy can vary nonmonotonically with the energy-arrival probability. I Introduction Timeliness is a key requirement in many communication systems, such as remote monitoring and networked control. The most widely used metric for it is the Age of Information (AoI). It was originally proposed in [ 2 ] and has since been analyzed in numerous communication systems [ 3 , 4 ] . It is defined, at a destination, as the time elapsed since the generation of the freshest data available at that destination [ 4 ] , i.e., I ⁡ ( t ) = t − u ⁡ ( t ) I(t)=t-u(t) , where u ⁡ ( t ) u(t) denotes the timestamp of the freshest received data, at or before time t t . Unlike delay, it captures both how often updates are sent and how long they take to arrive. However, AoI stops at reception. It implicitly assumes that a received update is immediately useful. In many systems, this is not the case. The received data is used to trigger an action at the destination [ 5 ] , and this action needs more than the data itself: a possibility , an enabling condition to put data into use. For example, an actuator powered by harvested energy can act only if its battery holds enough energy. An update that arrives when the battery is empty resets the AoI, yet no action takes place. The destination then holds fresh information, but its latest action is old. Moreover, a policy that minimizes the AoI may spend transmissions on updates that never translate into actions. Therefore, the freshness of the received data alone does not characterize the freshness of the actuations. Extensions of AoI have been proposed to capture semantic attributes and goal-oriented aspects of communication [ 6 , 5 ] , such as nonlinear aging costs [ 7 ] , version changes [ 8 ] , incorrect information [ 9 ] , and request- or query-based relevance [ 10 , 11 ] . The closest to actuation is Age of Loop (AoL), which extends AoI to closed-loop control by measuring the time since the generation of the state or command behind the latest applied action [ 12 ] . However, AoL assumes that actuation occurs periodically, with a fixed cycle. It does not model actuation as a constrained possibility that depends on a random process, such as the availability of energy. To capture this, we proposed Age of Actuation (AoA) [ 13 ] and later Age of Actuated Information (AoAI) [ 14 ] to go one step beyond AoI and analyze the broader case in which data requires a certain possibility (e.g., physical or admission-related) at the destination to be effectively utilized, and to assess the freshness of this final outcome. We refer to this concept as actuation . AoA is defined as the time elapsed since the most recent actuation at the destination ; its formal definition, together with that of the AoI, is given in Section II-B . I-A Related Work In a partial categorization, the analysis and optimization of AoI and, more generally, timeliness metrics can be divided into two main approaches: randomized (state-independent) policies and dynamic (state-dependent) policies. I-A 1 Randomized Policies They typically enable tractable analytical characterization, often modeling the system as an uncontrolled Markov chain, and can be interpreted as open-loop control. The decision policy is modeled as one or more random variables (RVs), usually Bernoulli RVs. After characterizing the system dynamics, one typically derives a closed-form expression for the timeliness metric (e.g., average AoI) as a function of the corresponding probability parameters of these RVs. In this approach, the policy does not depend on the system state; instead, at each time slot, decisions are made by sampling the RVs independently of the current system conditions [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . In our previous works, we utilized this approach [ 13 , 14 ] . I-A 2 Dynamic Policies They incorporate feedback from the system state, with decisions made at each time slot based on the current state of the system, such as age, channel conditions, and resource availability, thereby corresponding to closed-loop control. After decisions are made, the system transitions probabilistically to a new state according to its underlying dynamics. This sequential decision-making and the stochastic nature of the system lead to the formulation of the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), which provides a principled framework through the definition of states, actions, transition probabilities, and instant costs, typically correlating the cost with the age and minimizing the long-term cost which corresponds to the average AoI or related timeliness metrics. When the transition probabilities and instant costs are known, optimal policies can be computed using techniques such as value iteration, relative value iteration, or policy iteration, which rely on recursively solving the Bellman optimality equations. This approach has been applied to AoI minimization in energy harvesting systems with multiple sources [ 18 ] , wireless powered systems with joint sampling and updating [ 19 ] , and wireless broadcast networks [ 20 ] , and to version AoI in energy harvesting and caching systems [ 21 , 22 ] . AoI with an energy harvesting source has also been widely studied [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . Transmitting as soon as possible is not always age-optimal [ 28 ] , and this also holds under energy harvesting [ 23 ] . The optimal policy has a threshold structure in the age, shown in discrete time [ 24 ] , for a unit battery [ 25 ] , and for a finite battery with thresholds that decrease with the stored energy [ 26 ] . The average AoI of the greedy policy has also been derived in closed form [ 27 ] . In all these works, the optimized metric measures the freshness of the received data, not of its use. Moreover, in [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] , energy is consumed by the transmission itself. In our model, energy is instead needed at the destination for actuation. As a result, the AoI-optimal policy is to always transmit, and the threshold structure appears in the AoA-optimal policy instead. State-dependent policies have been used to optimize the freshness of received data, but not the freshness of actuation. On the other hand, the AoA has so far been studied only under state-independent randomized policies [ 13 , 14 ] . Thus, it is not known what an AoA-optimal state-dependent policy looks like, and whether and when it differs from the AoI-optimal policy. This paper addresses this gap. I-B Contribution In this work, we consider a system model that involves state-dependent decision-making to transmit data. We analyze the average AoA and the average AoI under both AoA-Optimal (AoA-Opt.) policy and AoI-Optimal (AoI-Opt.) policy. We thoroughly compare the outcomes and illustrate the trade-offs in timeliness and cost from the perspective of greedy and non-greedy regions, and show how the AoA captures the freshness of completed actuations and can therefore lead to a different optimal transmission policy from the AoI. The main contributions of the paper are as follows: • We characterize the AoA as an average-cost-per-stage problem and derive the optimal average AoA and the corresponding optimal policies using Relative Value Iteration (RVI). • We investigate structural properties of the MDP and prove an AoA-threshold structure for the AoA-Opt. policy , while such a structure for the battery state is observed only numerically. • We characterize the AoA for the AoI-Opt. (always-transmit) policy using a Markov chain formulation, derive its steady-state behavior, and obtain a closed-form expression for the average AoA under this policy. We also establish the ordering among the four values of the average AoA and the average AoI under the two policies. • We present and analyze two sets of operating regions, obtained by comparing the AoA-optimal and AoI-optimal policies, along with the resulting optimal and suboptimal values of the average AoA and the average AoI. • We present counterintuitive system behaviors that emerge at very low battery capacity, namely a battery capacity of one , such as a transmission rate that varies nonmonotonically with the energy-arrival probability.
